old_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law 6, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards.
new_digest: One Wicket shall be pitched, as in Law G, with a Bowling Stump opposite to it, at a distance of twenty-two yards.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the oft and leg stump.

old_digest: The ball must be hit before the Bounds to entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.
new_digest: The ball must be hit before the Bounds io entitle the Striker to a run, which run cannot he obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease.

old_digest: When the Striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground behind the poppin" crease, otherwise the Umpire shall call “No Hit,” and no run-shall be scored.
new_digest: When the Striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground behind the popping crease, otherwise the Umpire shall call “No Hit,” and no run shall he scored.

old_digest: The Striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost ball, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a fieldsman otherwise than with any part of his person.
new_digest: The Striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost hall, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a fieldsman otherwise than with any part of his person.

old_digest: A bowler may bowl with both feet behind the bowling crease provided that one foot is within the return crease. If a bowler knock the wicket with is foot in delivering the ball and remove a bail, such act does not in itself justify an Umpire in calling “No Ball.”
new_digest: Notes on Law 11. /V howler may howl with both feet behind the bowling crease provided that one foot is within the return crease. I f a howler knock the wicket with is foot in delivering the ball and remove a bail, such net does not in itself justify an Umpire in calling “No Ball.”

old_digest: If he delivers with the heel raised off the ground and keeps that part of the foot which is on the ground within the return ciease the delivery is allowed as fair.
new_digest: If he delivers with the heel raised off the ground and keeps that jwirt of the foot which is on the ground within the return crease the delivery is allowed as fair.

old_digest: When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the run was made. When a wide is called the ball does not on that account become “dead” and the batsman may be out stumped or run out.
new_digest: When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the rim was made. When a wide is called the ball does noton that account become “dead” and the batsman may be out stumped or run out.

old_digest: An over should always be finished, unless a wicket fall within two minutes of time (see Law 45), or unless there is a local rule extending the time.
new_digest: An over should always he finished, unless a wicket fall within two minutes of time (see Law 45), or unless there is a local rule extending the lime.

old_digest: The Laws of Cricket clearly make a distinction between the wicket-keeper and the fieldsmen and between cases of “stumping” and “run out”
new_digest: The Laws of Cricket, dearly make a distinction between the wicket-keeper and the fieldsmen and between cases of “stumping” and “run out”

old_digest: When a run is made by the bat off a “No Ball” only the run to the batsman should be scored and not the “No Ball” as well.
new_digest: When a run is made by the bat oft'a “No Ball’’only the run to the batsman should be scored and not the “No Ball” as well.

old_digest: In 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, be not allowed in First Class Matches.” This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.
new_digest: Note on Law 18. lu 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, bo not allowed in First Class Matches.’ This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.

old_digest: A Batsman shall be held to be “out of his ground,” unless his bat in hand, or some part of his person be grounded within the line of the Popping Crease. 9
new_digest: A Batsman shall be held to be “out of his ground,” unless his bat in hand, or some part of his person be grounded within the line of the Popping Crease.

old_digest: (See Notes on Law 32.) When a fieldsman catches a ball and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire, to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground. When a Batsman plays a ball on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out.
new_digest: (See Notes on Law !J2.) When a fieldsman catches a hall and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground. When a Batsman plays a hall on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out.

old_digest: If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand of the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.” 10 It is sufficient for the wicket-keeper to remove one bail in order to run out or stump a batsman. It would not be out if he were to knock the bails off with his foot, or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.

It is sufficient for the wicket-keeper to remove one bail in order to run out or stump a batsman. It would not be out if he were to knock the bails oft' with his foot, or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.

new_digest: (See Law 16, Note 3.)

old_digest: Or, if the ball be struck or be stopped by any part of his person, and he wilfully strike it again, except it be done for the purpose of guarding his wicket, which he may do with his bat, or any part of his person, except his hands;—“Hit the ball twice.” 11 The fact that a run is attempted may be evidence of the batsman’s intention to take advantage of the second stroke and the Umpire is entitled to regard it as such, but it is not conclusive. If the ball has been lawfully struck twice and an overthrow is made, the batsmen are entitled to the runs which follow. (See also Law 22, Note 3.)

old_digest: It should be noted, especially in League and Saturday Matches, that Umpires are appointed “one for each end” and not one for each side. 6
new_digest: It should be noted, especially in League and Saturday Matches, that Umpires are appointed “one for each end” and not one for each side.

old_digest: When a run has been made off a no-ball the no-ball should be scored ( although the ball has been caught.
new_digest: When a run has been made off a no-ball the no-ball should be scored although the ball has been caught. 12

old_digest: If the Ball, whether struck with the bat or not, lodges in a Batsman’s Clothing, the ball shall become “Dead.”
new_digest: If the Ball, whether struck with the bat or not, lodges in a Batsman’s Clothing, the ball shall become “Dead.” 9

old_digest: He may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before th owing at the wicket or knocking off the bails. A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws.
new_digest: A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws, i.e. he may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off’ the bails.

old_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side.
new_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side. 13

old_digest: The Ball shall weigh not less than five ounces and a half, nor more than five ounces and three-quarters. It shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference.
new_digest: The Ball shall weigh not less than five ounces and a half, nor more than five ounces and three-quarters, it shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference.

old_digest: The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or if any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30.
new_digest: The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket. If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or if any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30.

old_digest: (See also Instructions to Umpires.)
new_digest: (See “Umpires”.) 11

old_digest: No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time.
new_digest: No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time. 15

old_digest: (See also Instructions to Umpires as to “ declaring.”) A declaration of a first innings does not prechide a second innings.
new_digest: (See also under Umpires as to “declaring.”) A declaration of a first innings does not preclude a second innings.

old_digest: Where there in no play on the first day of a three day match Laws 53 and 54 shall apply as if the match were a two day match, and if in a three day match there is no play on the first two days, Laws 53, 54 and Law 1 ‘ one day matches ’ shall apply as if the match were a one day match.
new_digest: Where there is no play on the first day of a three day match Laws 53 and 54 shall apply as if the match were a two day match, and if in a three day match there is no play on the first two days, Law 54 and Law ‘one day matches’ shall apply as if the match were a one day match. Where there is no play on the first day of a two-day match, Law ‘one day matches’ shall apply as if the match were a one-day match.

old_digest: It is the duty of the Captain to see that his side obtain this advantage. The ground in this law means “the pitch.” After the actual commencement of play the ground may be again protected when necessary and shall be protected every night during the continuation of a match, but the covering shall be removed each morning, if fine, at 7 o’clock a.m. The covering must not protect a larger area than 18ft by 12ft at each end, and must not protect more than 3ft 6in in front of the popping crease.
